title: Learning to Generate Reviews and Discovering Sentiment
abstract: We explore the properties of byte-level recurrent language models. When given sufficient amounts of capacity, training data, and compute time, the representations learned by these models include disentangled features corresponding to high-level concepts. Specifically, we find a single unit which performs sentiment analysis. These representations, learned in an unsupervised manner, achieve state of the art on the binary subset of the Stanford Sentiment Treebank. They are also very data efficient. When using only a handful of labeled examples, our approach matches the performance of strong baselines trained on full datasets. We also demonstrate the sentiment unit has a direct influence on the generative process of the model. Simply fixing its value to be positive or negative generates samples with the corresponding positive or negative sentiment.
research_question: Does unsupervised language modeling on a large, domain-specific corpus learn high-level, disentangled features, such as a unit corresponding to sentiment?
core_contribution: Training a byte-level recurrent language model on a large corpus of reviews leads to the unsupervised discovery of a single, interpretable unit that encodes sentiment, enabling state-of-the-art sentiment analysis and controllable text generation.
conclusion: Unsupervised language modeling can learn high-level, interpretable, and manipulable features like sentiment, demonstrating the potential of representation learning without explicit supervision.
key_findings: A single unit in the mLSTM's cell state strongly correlates with sentiment, achieving high accuracy on sentiment classification tasks.
The learned representation is highly data-efficient, matching strong supervised baselines with only a handful of labeled examples.
Fixing the value of the sentiment unit to positive or negative directly influences the sentiment of text generated by the model.
The model's performance plateaus on larger, out-of-domain datasets, indicating sensitivity to the training data distribution.
The model performs competitively on paraphrase detection but poorly on semantic relatedness tasks that are out-of-domain.
limitation: Performance plateaus on larger datasets and out-of-domain data (e.g., Yelp reviews vs. Amazon reviews).
The model is trained only on Amazon reviews, limiting its sensitivity to concepts in other domains.
The byte-level model may focus on the last few sentences instead of the whole document for longer texts.
The linear classifier on top of the static representation may saturate with more labeled data, limiting performance compared to more complex models.
future_direction: Improving the representation model in terms of architecture and size.
Developing hierarchical/multi-timescale extensions to improve representations for longer documents.
Training on a wider mix of datasets to improve coverage of target tasks.
